title: Cross-era figures: source, transmission and later reception
question: How are Laozi, Confucius and Śākyamuni understood across different times, places, texts and later institutions?
disclaimer: This is a comparison built from the current relations and sources; it does not collapse three figures, three traditions or different evidence layers into one historical fact.

entities.title: Laozi (Li Er)
entities.timeLabel: Traditionally placed in the late Spring and Autumn period; dates contested
entities.summary: Laozi is a recognisable gateway into Daoist classicism, but the Li Er biography, the sage-name Laozi, the formation of the Daodejing and the later Taishang Laojun image must remain distinct layers.

entities.title: Confucius (Kong Qiu)
entities.summary: Confucius is a recognisable gateway into Confucian classics, education and political ethics; sayings in the Analects must be separated from disciple records, compilation layers and later classical reception.

entities.title: Śākyamuni Buddha (Gautama)
entities.timeLabel: Traditional and scholarly dates contested; broad fifth-century BCE navigation range
entities.summary: Śākyamuni is a central gateway into Buddhist thought and pilgrimage geography, but fragmentary early-text biographies, later Buddha legends and sacred narratives must remain layered.

bridges.title: Confucius visits Zhou to ask Laozi about rites
summaries: The Shiji places Laozi in the narrative of Confucius asking about rites in Zhou; this retains the historiographical and traditional layer rather than treating the encounter as independently verified field evidence.
The Shiji preserves the rites-asking story as a historiographical entry into a Dao–Ru encounter; exact dating and dialogue details remain traditional.

bridges.title: Luoyang
summaries: Laozi is connected in historiographical tradition with the Zhou archive and rites-asking narrative; Luoyang is used as a city-scale traditional context, not as a precise residence claim.
The historiographical account of Confucius asking about rites in Zhou can use Luoyang as a city-scale spatial entry without reconstructing a certain travel route.
